hints: Start by counting the regions of electron density around each carbon in $\text{C}_6\text{H}_6$ to decide the hybridisation.
Remember benzene has two different types of bonding between carbons, one in the plane and one above and below the plane.
Link each bond type to the specific orbitals that overlap, $\text{sp}^2$ with $\text{sp}^2$, p with p, and $\text{sp}^2$ with s for $\text{C-H}$.
walkthrough:
Fix the hybridisation first**
Picture each carbon in benzene. It is joined to two other carbons and one hydrogen, three sigma regions in a flat trigonal arrangement. That is the classic signature of $\text{sp}^2$ hybridisation. Each carbon therefore keeps one unhybridised p orbital perpendicular to the ring.

Sort out C to C bonding**
Between any two carbons there is a strong $\sigma$ bond in the plane of the ring. Think of it as $\text{sp}^2$ meeting $\text{sp}^2$ head on. Above and below the plane the six p orbitals overlap sideways to give the $\pi$ system, delocalised around the whole ring. So C to C involves both $\sigma$ and $\pi$.

Sort out C to H bonding**
The bond to hydrogen is much simpler. It is a single $\sigma$ bond only, no pi character. It is made when the remaining $\text{sp}^2$ orbital on carbon overlaps head on with the 1s orbital on hydrogen.

Final answer: All six C atoms are $\text{sp}^2$ hybridised.
C to C bonds consist of one $\sigma$ bond and one $\pi$ bond contribution from the delocalised system. $\text{C-C}$ $\sigma$ bonds are formed by overlap of $\text{sp}^2$ hybrid orbitals, $\text{C-C}$ $\pi$ bonds are formed by overlap of unhybridised p orbitals.
C to H bonds are $\sigma$ bonds formed by overlap of C $\text{sp}^2$ hybrid orbital with H 1s orbital.

hints: Step 1 converts benzene to methylbenzene, so identify which reagent can supply a $\text{CH}_3$ electrophile with the help of a Lewis acid catalyst.
walkthrough:
Spot the alkylation**
You are adding a $\text{CH}_3$ group directly to the ring. That is Friedel-Crafts alkylation. You need a chloroalkane to generate the carbocation-like electrophile, so $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$, plus the classic Lewis acid carrier $\text{AlCl}_3$ to polarise it and form $^+\text{CH}_3$.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$ and $\text{AlCl}_3$ (Friedel-Crafts alkylation, anhydrous conditions).

hints: Recall that the benzene pi system acts as the nucleophile that attacks the $^+\text{CH}_3$ electrophile in the first step.
Think about what the ring looks like after it has accepted the electrophile, charge and delocalisation of the positive charge.
Consider how aromaticity is restored by removal of the ring proton and what the second product must be besides methylbenzene.
walkthrough:
Electrophilic attack**
Think of the delocalised pi cloud as electron rich. It donates a pair to the electron deficient $^+\text{CH}_3$. Draw your first curly arrow starting inside the hexagon and pointing to the $^+\text{CH}_3$, making a new $\text{C-C}$ bond. The ring now loses its full aromaticity.

Draw the intermediate correctly**
You now have a cyclohexadienyl cation, often called the Wheland intermediate. One carbon is tetrahedral and carries the $\text{CH}_3$ and H. The positive charge is delocalised over the other five carbons, shown with a horseshoe of three double bonds and a + sign. Keep the $\text{CH}_3$ clearly attached.

Restore aromaticity**
Aromaticity is very stable, so the system wants it back. A base removes the proton on the same carbon that carries the $\text{CH}_3$. Draw a curly arrow from that $\text{C-H}$ bond back into the ring to reform the pi system. The $\text{H}^+$ leaves, and you get methylbenzene plus $\text{H}^+$.

Final answer: Curly arrow from pi system inside benzene ring to $^+\text{CH}_3$ to form C-C bond.
Wheland intermediate with $\text{CH}_3$ attached, one $\text{sp}^3$ carbon, delocalised positive charge shown with horseshoe and + in ring.
Curly arrow from $\text{C-H}$ bond at the $\text{sp}^3$ carbon back into ring to reform aromatic pi system, giving $\text{H}^+$ as second product.

hints: Step 2 adds an $\text{NO}_2$ group to methylbenzene, so recall the two strong acids that generate the $\text{NO}_2^+$ electrophile.
Remember both acids must be concentrated and the mixture must be kept cool to avoid multiple nitration.
walkthrough:
Name the nitrating mixture**
You are putting $\text{NO}_2$ onto the ring. That always needs the nitrating mixture. Concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$ provides the source of nitrogen, concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ acts as the stronger acid to generate the true electrophile $\text{NO}_2^+$ plus water.

Control the conditions**
Both acids must be concentrated, not dilute. Heat gently but keep the temperature low, typically about $50 ^\circ\text{C}$ and within the $25$ to $60 ^\circ\text{C}$ range. Too hot gives dinitration, too cold gives no reaction. Here the $\text{CH}_3$ group activates the ring and directs para.

Final answer: Concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$ and concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$.
Temperature $25 ^\circ\text{C} \leqslant \text{T} \leqslant 60 ^\circ\text{C}$, with cooling.

hints: Step 3 oxidises the $\text{CH}_3$ side chain to $\text{COOH}$ while leaving the ring and $\text{NO}_2$ untouched, so think of the strong alkaline oxidiser used for alkylbenzenes.
walkthrough:
Recognise side chain oxidation**
Look at the change: $\text{CH}_3$ becomes $\text{COOH}$. The benzene ring survives. That is the classic vigorous oxidation of an alkyl side chain with hot alkaline $\text{KMnO}_4$. Acid work up then gives the free benzoic acid W.
Final answer: Alkaline $\text{KMnO}_4$, heated under reflux, followed by acidification.

hints: Name the disubstituted benzene W with $\text{NO}_2$ and $\text{COOH}$ in para positions, giving priority to the acid as the parent.
walkthrough:
Apply benzoic acid naming**
The parent is benzoic acid because $\text{COOH}$ has priority. Number so $\text{COOH}$ is carbon 1. The $\text{NO}_2$ is opposite it, at position 4. Hence 4-nitrobenzoic acid, the para isomer.
Final answer: 4-nitrobenzoic acid.

hints: Step 4 reduces $\text{NO}_2$ to $\text{NH}_2$ without reducing $\text{COOH}$, so recall the metal plus hot concentrated acid system that is selective for nitro groups.
walkthrough:
Choose a selective reducing agent**
You must reduce nitro to amine but keep the carboxylic acid intact. $\text{LiAlH}_4$ would attack $\text{COOH}$, so avoid it. Hot tin metal with concentrated $\text{HCl}$ cleanly reduces $\text{Ar-NO}_2$ to $\text{Ar-NH}_2$ and leaves $\text{COOH}$ alone. Alkali work up then liberates the free amine X.
Final answer: Sn and hot concentrated $\text{HCl}$, followed by neutralisation with $\text{NaOH}$.

hints: Compare X and Y, X has $\text{NH}_2$ para to $\text{COOH}$ while Y has them meta to each other, so think about which group present during nitration controls para versus meta.
Recall that $\text{CH}_3$ is 2,4-directing but $\text{COOH}$ and $\text{NO}_2$ are 3-directing, and decide when the oxidising step must occur to get meta nitration.
walkthrough:
See why the original order gives para**
In Fig. 9.1 nitration happens on methylbenzene. $\text{CH}_3$ is activating and 2,4-directing, so $\text{NO}_2^+$ goes para to $\text{CH}_3$. After oxidation and reduction you keep that para relationship in X.

Swap to get meta**
Compound Y needs the $\text{NH}_2$ (from $\text{NO}_2$) meta to $\text{COOH}$. Do the oxidation first: benzene to methylbenzene, then oxidise $\text{CH}_3$ to $\text{COOH}$ to give benzoic acid, then nitrate. $\text{COOH}$ is deactivating and 3-directing, so it directs $\text{NO}_2^+$ to the meta position. Reduction then gives 3-aminobenzoic acid, which is Y.

Final answer: Perform step 3 before step 2.
$\text{COOH}$ is 3-directing (meta directing) so nitration of benzoic acid gives the 3-nitro isomer, which on reduction gives compound Y.
